questions.stem: What are the units of rate of reaction when concentration is tracked?

options.text: mol dm-3 s-1
options.explanation: Rate is a concentration change per time, so concentration units divide by seconds.

options.text: mol dm-3
options.explanation: That is a concentration, not a change in concentration over time.
That would suit a first-order rate constant, not a rate measured in concentration terms.

options.text: g s-1
options.explanation: Mass-based rates are possible experimentally, but the defined rate unit here is concentration per time.

questions.stem: Which property change could NOT follow the course of the reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g)?

options.text: A colour change as E accumulates
options.explanation: Colour tracks concentration whenever the mixture changes appearance.

options.text: A constant electrical conductivity reading
options.explanation: Conductivity only carries rate information when ion concentrations change; here it stays constant, so it cannot follow the course.

options.text: A fall in the volume of D present in the mixture
options.explanation: D is aqueous and its concentration changes as it reacts, so tracking it is sensible.

options.text: The mass of the reaction vessel and contents
options.explanation: Mass follows the escape of gaseous F, so it changes measurably.

questions.stem: Rate of reaction is calculated by dividing

options.text: The time taken by the temperature rise
options.explanation: Temperature is not the defined quantity here and the ratio is inverted.

options.text: The concentration of product by the concentration of reactant
options.explanation: That compares two concentrations at one instant, not a change over time.

options.text: The change in concentration of a reactant or product by the time taken for that change
options.explanation: The definition is concentration change per unit time.

options.text: The total volume of product by the total mass of reactant
options.explanation: Neither ratio carries time, so neither is a rate.

questions.stem: Gas volume collected over time is a valid rate measurement because

options.text: Gas volume always equals the volume of solution used
options.explanation: There is no such equality in rate work.

options.text: Gases dissolve completely in the solution
options.explanation: Collected gases are assumed not to dissolve significantly.

options.text: Volume is independent of the reaction
options.explanation: The whole point is that gas volume grows as reaction proceeds.

options.text: The volume of gas produced is proportional to the amount of product formed
options.explanation: Gas moles map directly onto product amount through the equation.

questions.stem: A student measures the mass of a flask at 10-second intervals as carbon dioxide escapes. The mass readings give rate information because

options.text: The falling mass measures reactant or mixture amount at each instant, so differences between readings measure change over time
options.explanation: Successive mass readings give concentration-equivalent changes over measured intervals.

options.text: Mass and volume are identical quantities
options.explanation: They are distinct physical quantities.

options.text: The balance itself changes the rate
options.explanation: Weighing does not alter the reaction.

options.text: Mass loss equals rate directly without any calculation
options.explanation: A mass reading is an amount, not a rate; rate needs the change divided by time.

questions.stem: State the definition of rate of reaction and its units.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate of reaction is the concentration change of a chosen reactant or product divided by the time interval, recorded in mol dm-3 s-1.

questions.stem: List three measurable changes that can be used to follow the rate of a reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Any three of: mass lost over time, volume of gas produced, colour change or colorimetry, pH change, or electrical conductivity change.

questions.stem: Explain why the model reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g) is convenient for studying rate at different concentrations of D.
questions.modelAnswer: The gaseous product F can be collected so its volume tracks progress directly, while D stays in solution where samples of known concentration can be prepared, so rates at several starting concentrations of D can be measured and tabulated side by side.

questions.stem: A reaction liberates hydrogen gas, but a student proposes monitoring it by colour change. Comment on the suitability and suggest a better measurement.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen and its solutions are colourless, so no colour signal develops and colorimetry would read a flat line; collecting the hydrogen volume in a gas syringe instead gives a directly proportional measure of product formed against time.

questions.stem: The data for D show that doubling [D] doubles the rate. The rate expression is therefore

options.text: rate = k[D] raised to a fractional power
options.explanation: Fractional orders exist but this clean doubling shows power one.

options.text: rate = k[D], first order in D
options.explanation: Direct proportionality means a power of one on [D].

options.text: rate = k[D]2, second order in D
options.explanation: Squaring would make doubling concentration quadruple the rate.

options.text: rate = k, zero order in D
options.explanation: Zero order would leave rate unchanged as [D] moves.

questions.stem: In the rate equation rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, the values of m and n

options.text: Are always 1 and 1
options.explanation: Orders take zero, positive and sometimes fractional values.

options.text: Are fixed by the temperature
options.explanation: Temperature changes k, not the orders.

options.text: Must be determined experimentally
options.explanation: Orders are kinetic facts that only measurement reveals.

options.text: Equal the balancing coefficients of A and B
options.explanation: Stoichiometry does not fix orders.

questions.stem: Which species may legitimately appear in a rate equation?

options.text: Any intermediate formed and consumed en route
options.explanation: Intermediates are excluded from rate equations.

options.text: Only gaseous reactants
options.explanation: Rate equations include whatever the mechanism involves, whatever its state.

options.text: Every species in the stoichiometric equation
options.explanation: Being in the overall equation does not guarantee a rate role.

options.text: A catalyst used in the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysts can feature because they affect the rate-determining chemistry.

questions.stem: The rate constant k in rate = k[D] is best described as

options.text: The proportionality constant connecting rate to the concentrations raised to their powers
options.explanation: k glues the concentration terms to the rate.

options.text: A second rate measured in different units
options.explanation: k is not itself a rate.

options.text: A quantity that rises when more D is added
options.explanation: Changing concentration moves along the expression; k is unchanged.

options.text: A fixed universal constant for all reactions
options.explanation: k is characteristic of each reaction and changes with temperature.

questions.stem: Rate equations can only be determined experimentally because

options.text: Rate equations change during a run
options.explanation: The rate equation is fixed for a given reaction and temperature.

options.text: The orders describe mechanism behaviour that the stoichiometric equation does not encode
options.explanation: Balancing numbers say nothing about the slow-step chemistry that sets orders.

options.text: Concentrations cannot be measured
options.explanation: Concentrations are routinely measured in kinetics work.

options.text: k changes during every experiment
options.explanation: k stays constant at fixed temperature.

questions.stem: State the rate expression for the reaction where rate is proportional to [D].
questions.modelAnswer: Rate = k[D], with k the rate constant and the reaction first order with respect to D.

questions.stem: Write the general rate equation for A plus B giving C plus D, naming each symbol.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant, [A] and [B] are reactant concentrations, and m and n are the orders with respect to A and B.

questions.stem: Explain why an intermediate does not feature in a rate equation even though it takes part in the chemistry.
questions.modelAnswer: An intermediate is made and consumed inside the mechanism rather than supplied by the chemist, so its concentration is not an independent variable; the rate equation is expressed in terms of what is actually added and controlled, which is why intermediates are absent.

questions.stem: A reaction's stoichiometric equation shows 2A plus B forming products, yet experiment gives rate = k[A]. Reconcile the two statements.
questions.modelAnswer: The balancing numbers and the kinetic orders are independent: the experiment shows the rate depends only on one power of A, so the slow chemistry involves A but not free B; the coefficient 2 in the overall equation is bookkeeping, not an order, and the rate equation from experiment stands.
